lessonTitle: Early Pregnancy Loss and Antepartum Haemorrhage

blocks.text: A 26-year-old woman, six weeks after her last period, faints in a supermarket queue. She has dull left iliac fossa pain, light brown vaginal loss and pain at the tip of her right shoulder. Her pulse is 122 beats per minute and her abdomen is tender and guarded. A pregnancy test is positive. Within minutes the question is not 'what type of bleeding is this?' but 'where is the pregnancy, and how much blood has she lost?'

blocks.markdown:
Bleeding in pregnancy is divided by gestation. **Before viability** it is called early pregnancy bleeding and, if the pregnancy is lost before 24 completed weeks (the UK threshold of viability), it is a **miscarriage**. **After 24 weeks, and before birth**, it is an **antepartum haemorrhage (APH)**. The two share one practical priority: decide quickly whether the woman is haemodynamically stable, because that decides whether you investigate first or resuscitate first.

In early pregnancy the key anatomical question is **intrauterine or extrauterine**. A transvaginal ultrasound scan (TVS) can usually show an intrauterine gestational sac with a yolk sac from about 5 to 6 weeks, and a fetal pole with cardiac activity shortly afterwards.

blocks.title: Miscarriage and ectopic pregnancy
blocks.text: Miscarriage is the spontaneous loss of an intrauterine pregnancy before 24 completed weeks. An ectopic pregnancy is one in which the fertilised ovum implants outside the uterine cavity, most often in the ampulla of the fallopian tube. A pregnancy of unknown location (PUL) is a positive pregnancy test with no pregnancy visible on scan; it is a working label, not a diagnosis.

rows: Viable intrauterine pregnancy with cardiac activity
Intrauterine sac, may or may not have cardiac activity
Bleeding and pain, some tissue passed
Retained products of conception in the cavity
Bleeding and pain settling after passing tissue
Empty uterus, thin endometrium, previously confirmed intrauterine pregnancy
Often none, or brown loss; symptoms of pregnancy fade
Embryo without cardiac activity, or empty sac above size thresholds
blocks.caption: Types of miscarriage. A confirmed intrauterine pregnancy previously seen on scan is needed before labelling a miscarriage complete.

blocks.markdown: UK guidance (NICE and the RCOG) uses cautious ultrasound thresholds because a mistaken diagnosis of pregnancy loss could end a wanted pregnancy. On TVS a **crown-rump length (CRL) of 7.0 mm or more with no cardiac activity**, or a **mean gestational sac diameter (MSD) of 25 mm or more with no embryo**, indicates a non-viable pregnancy. Below these thresholds, the scan is repeated after at least a week. Management of a confirmed miscarriage is **expectant** (wait, usually 7 to 14 days), **medical** (misoprostol, with mifepristone pre-treatment for a missed miscarriage) or **surgical** (manual vacuum aspiration or suction evacuation). Rhesus-negative women are assessed for anti-D immunoglobulin according to local guideline, mainly after surgical management and later gestations.

blocks.title: Interpreting a scan report
blocks.prompt: A woman at 9 weeks by dates has light bleeding and a closed os. TVS shows an intrauterine fetal pole with CRL 9 mm and no cardiac activity. What is the diagnosis, and which type of miscarriage is it?

steps.text: Locate the pregnancy: a fetal pole is visible inside the uterine cavity, so this is an intrauterine pregnancy and ectopic pregnancy is not the primary concern.
Apply the viability threshold: the CRL is 9 mm, which is at or above 7.0 mm, and there is no cardiac activity.

Conclude: the embryo has died but nothing has been expelled and the os is closed, so this is a missed (delayed) miscarriage. A second sonographer or repeat scan is commonly used to confirm, then options are offered: expectant, medical or surgical.

blocks.answer: Missed (delayed) miscarriage, because a CRL of 7.0 mm or more with no cardiac activity indicates a non-viable intrauterine pregnancy with a closed os.

blocks.markdown: **Ectopic pregnancy** classically presents between 6 and 8 weeks with amenorrhoea, lower abdominal pain and light dark vaginal bleeding. Shoulder-tip pain arises from diaphragmatic irritation by free blood. Risk factors are previous ectopic pregnancy, tubal surgery or pelvic inflammatory disease, previous sterilisation, an intrauterine contraceptive device in situ and assisted conception, but about half of women have none. On TVS you may see an empty uterus with an adnexal mass and free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. When the scan shows no pregnancy anywhere, the woman has a PUL and is followed with serial serum hCG measurements. A **ruptured ectopic with shock** needs resuscitation and emergency laparoscopy or laparotomy, not further imaging. A stable woman with a small unruptured tubal ectopic and low hCG may have methotrexate or expectant management; otherwise surgery (salpingectomy, or salpingostomy if the other tube is damaged and fertility is a priority) is used.

**Antepartum haemorrhage** has two classic placental causes. In **placenta praevia** the placenta lies low and covers or lies within 20 mm of the internal cervical os, so the lower segment stretches as it forms and the placenta shears off. In **placental abruption** a normally sited placenta separates before delivery, typically after bleeding at the decidua basalis. Bleeding can be **revealed** (through the vagina) or **concealed** (trapped as a retroplacental clot), so visible blood loss can badly underestimate true loss.

rows: Dark; may be small or absent if concealed
Fetus usually well until large loss
Previous caesarean section, multiple pregnancy, previous praevia
Hypertension, pre-eclampsia, trauma, smoking, cocaine, previous abruption
blocks.caption: Placenta praevia versus placental abruption.

blocks.title: No digital vaginal examination
blocks.text: Never perform a digital vaginal examination in a woman with APH until a placenta praevia has been excluded by ultrasound. A finger can disrupt the placenta and cause torrential bleeding. A sterile speculum examination is safe once a praevia is excluded or when the clinician is prepared for immediate delivery.

blocks.title: Quantifying a haemorrhage with the shock index
blocks.prompt: A woman of 62 kg at 35 weeks has a sudden painful APH. Pulse is 112 beats per minute and systolic blood pressure is 98 mmHg. Calculate the shock index and judge the severity. Assume blood volume in pregnancy is about 100 mL/kg.

steps.text: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure (SI).
Interpret: a normal SI is about 0.5 to 0.7. A value of 0.9 or more in obstetric practice is a warning sign, and a value above 1.0 suggests significant haemorrhage and possible concealed loss.
Estimate the circulating volume to frame the loss.
Act: because the SI exceeds 1.0 a major haemorrhage response is triggered even if little blood is visible.

blocks.answer: Shock index approximately 1.14 with a circulating volume of about 6200 mL, so treat as significant haemorrhage and start resuscitation.

blocks.markdown: **Resuscitating major obstetric haemorrhage** runs ABC, in parallel, with a team. Call for senior help immediately (obstetrician, anaesthetist, midwife in charge, haematologist) and activate the major obstetric haemorrhage protocol. Give high-flow oxygen, position the woman in left lateral tilt after 20 weeks so the gravid uterus does not compress the inferior vena cava, and place **two large-bore (14G or 16G) intravenous cannulae**. Take bloods for full blood count, group and crossmatch, coagulation including **fibrinogen**, and urea and electrolytes. Give warmed crystalloid initially to restore perfusion, move early to **blood and blood products** (group-specific or O-negative if urgent), and consider **tranexamic acid** (teaching example: 1 g intravenously over 10 minutes). Keep her warm, monitor pulse, blood pressure, urine output and oxygen saturation, and keep a written record of blood loss. Because the placenta or uterus is the source, **definitive treatment is delivery**, usually by emergency caesarean section if the mother or fetus is compromised.

items: Call for help and activate the major haemorrhage protocol.
Airway, oxygen, left lateral tilt, two large-bore cannulae.
Send bloods including crossmatch and fibrinogen.
Replace volume with warmed fluids, then blood and products guided by results.
Give tranexamic acid and correct coagulopathy.
Control the source, usually by delivery, and give anti-D to rhesus-negative women.

blocks.title: Treat the woman, not the visible blood
blocks.text: In abruption the blood may be entirely concealed, so tachycardia, a rising shock index or a hard tender uterus should trigger resuscitation regardless of how little blood is seen. In early pregnancy any shocked woman with a positive pregnancy test has a ruptured ectopic until proven otherwise.

points: Miscarriage types are separated by os status, tissue passed and TVS findings; CRL of 7.0 mm or more with no cardiac activity, or MSD of 25 mm or more with no embryo, confirms non-viability.
Ectopic pregnancy presents with pain, amenorrhoea and bleeding; a shocked woman needs resuscitation and surgery, not more imaging.
Placenta praevia gives painless fresh bleeding with a soft uterus, whereas abruption gives painful dark or concealed bleeding with a hard uterus, shock out of proportion and risk of DIC.
Major haemorrhage resuscitation: help, ABC, two large cannulae, bloods and crossmatch, warmed fluids then blood products, tranexamic acid, and delivery to remove the source.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman at 12 weeks by dates has had two days of spotting and no pain. Her os is closed. TVS shows an intrauterine fetal pole with CRL 15 mm and no cardiac activity. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Threatened miscarriage
Complete miscarriage
Missed (delayed) miscarriage
Pregnancy of unknown location

distractorRationale.a: A threatened miscarriage has a viable pregnancy with cardiac activity.
distractorRationale.b: In a complete miscarriage the uterus is empty; here the fetal pole is still in the cavity.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: CRL of 7.0 mm or more with no cardiac activity and a closed os indicates a missed miscarriage.
distractorRationale.d: A PUL means no pregnancy is seen on scan; here an intrauterine pregnancy is visible.

questions.explanation: The pregnancy is clearly intrauterine and the CRL of 15 mm exceeds the 7.0 mm threshold, yet there is no heartbeat, so the embryo is non-viable. Because the os is closed and nothing has been expelled, this is a missed miscarriage rather than inevitable or incomplete.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 34 weeks presents with a small amount of bright red vaginal bleeding that woke her from sleep. She has no pain. The uterus is soft and non-tender and the fetus is in a transverse lie, with a normal fetal heart rate. She had one previous caesarean section. Which action is most appropriate before the placental site is known?

options.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination to assess cervical dilatation
Avoid digital examination and arrange an urgent ultrasound scan to locate the placenta
Commence oxytocin to induce labour
Perform amniotomy to assess the colour of the liquor

questions.correctOptionText: Avoid digital examination and arrange an urgent ultrasound scan to locate the placenta

distractorRationale.a: Digital examination can provoke massive bleeding if the placenta is praevia.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: painless fresh bleeding, soft uterus, malpresentation and a previous caesarean all suggest placenta praevia, so image first.
distractorRationale.c: Induction is inappropriate and dangerous if the placenta covers the os.
distractorRationale.d: Amniotomy requires a vaginal examination and would risk haemorrhage.

questions.explanation: Painless bright bleeding with a soft uterus, a transverse lie and a prior caesarean scar is the classic picture of placenta praevia. A digital examination could disrupt placental tissue over the os, so the placental site is established by ultrasound first.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old at 36 weeks, with chronic hypertension, develops sudden constant abdominal pain after a fall at home. There is only a small amount of dark vaginal blood. Her pulse is 124 beats per minute, blood pressure is 96/60 mmHg, the uterus is hard and tender, and the fetal heart rate shows a bradycardia. Which finding best explains why her shock is more severe than the visible loss?

options.text: Revealed bleeding from a low-lying placenta
Concealed retroplacental haemorrhage from placental abruption
Cervical ectropion bleeding
Vasa praevia with fetal blood loss only

questions.correctOptionText: Concealed retroplacental haemorrhage from placental abruption

distractorRationale.a: Praevia bleeding is painless and the uterus is soft; shock is in proportion to visible loss.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: hypertension and trauma are risk factors for abruption and blood can be trapped behind the placenta.
distractorRationale.c: Ectropion causes minor bleeding and does not cause shock or uterine tenderness.
distractorRationale.d: Vasa praevia threatens the fetus but does not cause maternal shock.

questions.explanation: A hard, tender uterus with pain, risk factors (hypertension and trauma) and shock out of proportion to visible loss point to abruption with concealed haemorrhage. Concealed blood within the uterus can reach large volumes without appearing at the introitus.

questions.stem: A woman of 28 weeks has had a heavy APH and is tachycardic and pale. Which is the most appropriate first step in managing her care?

options.text: Request an outpatient ultrasound scan within 48 hours
Call senior obstetric, anaesthetic and midwifery help, activate the major haemorrhage protocol and site two large-bore cannulae
Give oral iron and review in clinic
Perform a digital vaginal examination to find the source of bleeding

questions.correctOptionText: Call senior obstetric, anaesthetic and midwifery help, activate the major haemorrhage protocol and site two large-bore cannulae

distractorRationale.a: Delay is unsafe in a shocked patient.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: resuscitation is multidisciplinary and parallel, starting with help, ABC and access.
distractorRationale.c: Oral iron is not an acute treatment for haemorrhage.
distractorRationale.d: Digital examination is contraindicated until praevia is excluded and does not help resuscitation.

questions.explanation: Major obstetric haemorrhage is managed by a team working in parallel, so calling for help, activating the protocol and obtaining wide-bore access come first. Investigations and definitive treatment follow while volume is being restored.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old with 7 weeks of amenorrhoea has mild left-sided pelvic pain and light bleeding. She is haemodynamically stable. Serum hCG is positive. TVS shows an empty uterus, no adnexal mass and no free fluid. What is the most appropriate label and plan?

options.text: Complete miscarriage; discharge with no follow-up
Confirmed ectopic pregnancy; give methotrexate immediately
Pregnancy of unknown location; follow with serial hCG and safety-net advice
Threatened miscarriage; reassure and repeat scan in 12 weeks

questions.correctOptionText: Pregnancy of unknown location; follow with serial hCG and safety-net advice

distractorRationale.a: A complete miscarriage requires a previously confirmed intrauterine pregnancy; here none has been seen.
distractorRationale.b: An ectopic is not confirmed without visualising an extrauterine pregnancy and a PUL should not be treated as one.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: a positive test with no visible pregnancy is a PUL, followed by serial hCG and clear safety-net advice because ectopic cannot be excluded.
distractorRationale.d: Threatened miscarriage needs a visible viable intrauterine pregnancy.

questions.explanation: Without any visible pregnancy the correct label is PUL, which keeps ectopic pregnancy on the differential. The woman is followed with repeat hCG and told to return urgently if pain worsens or she feels faint.

questions.stem: A woman at 33 weeks with an APH has a pulse of 126 beats per minute and a systolic blood pressure of 84 mmHg. Calculate her shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure; give the answer as a number with no unit, to two decimal places).
questions.explanation: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure, so 126 divided by 84 equals 1.50. A value this far above 1.0 indicates major haemorrhage and should trigger the major haemorrhage protocol.

questions.stem: A woman weighing 80 kg at 37 weeks is taken to theatre for a placenta praevia caesarean section. Take her circulating blood volume as 100 mL/kg. Anaesthetic records show she has lost 20 percent of her blood volume. How many millilitres of blood has she lost (answer in mL)?
questions.explanation: Circulating volume is 80 multiplied by 100, giving 8000 mL, and 20 percent of this is 1600 mL. A loss of this size should prompt blood product replacement and early involvement of the haematologist.

questions.stem: True or false: In placental abruption the amount of visible vaginal bleeding reliably reflects the total blood loss.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Abruption can be concealed with blood collecting behind the placenta, so visible loss may be small while maternal shock and coagulopathy are severe. Clinical signs such as pain, tachycardia and a hard uterus are more reliable than visible blood.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman at 32 weeks arrives at the delivery suite with a heavy APH, a pulse of 130 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg. Outline the initial resuscitation and the principle of definitive management.
markingGuide: Call senior obstetric, anaesthetic, midwifery and haematology help and activate the major obstetric haemorrhage protocol
High-flow oxygen and left lateral tilt (uterine displacement)
Bloods: FBC, group and crossmatch, coagulation screen with fibrinogen, urea and electrolytes
Warmed crystalloid then early blood and blood products (O-negative or group-specific if urgent)
Tranexamic acid (1 g IV given as a teaching example)
Continuous monitoring: pulse, blood pressure, urine output, saturations, and accurate blood loss recording
Definitive treatment is delivery, usually emergency caesarean section if mother or fetus is compromised, with anti-D for rhesus-negative women
questions.explanation: Major obstetric haemorrhage is managed with simultaneous resuscitation, source control and monitoring. Because the bleeding originates from the placental bed, volume replacement buys time but delivery is the definitive treatment.

questions.stem: Contrast placenta praevia and placental abruption in a woman presenting with APH, covering the history, abdominal examination, expected fetal findings and the main risk factors of each.
markingGuide: Praevia: painless bright red bleeding; abruption: constant severe pain with dark or concealed blood
Praevia: soft non-tender uterus; abruption: hard (woody) tender uterus
Praevia: malpresentation or high presenting part; abruption: normal presentation but fetal distress or death is common
Shock proportional to visible loss in praevia; out of proportion in concealed abruption
Coagulopathy (DIC) is characteristic of severe abruption
Praevia risk factors: previous caesarean section, multiple pregnancy, previous praevia
Abruption risk factors: hypertension or pre-eclampsia, trauma, smoking, cocaine, previous abruption
No digital vaginal examination until praevia is excluded by ultrasound
questions.explanation: The two conditions differ in mechanism: praevia bleeds from a low placenta that cannot adapt to lower segment stretch, while abruption involves separation of a normally sited placenta with retroplacental clot. These mechanisms explain painless versus painful bleeding and soft versus hard uterus.
